question: The thermal buffer is at 67°C at 14:00. Should I run the dishwasher now or wait?
answer: Yes, run the dishwasher now. The buffer top is at 67°C, well above the minimum usable temperature of around 55°C for domestic hot water. PV is currently producing 3.84 kW, which covers a typical dishwasher load of 1.8–2.2 kW entirely from solar. The collector at 78.3°C means the buffer will continue charging through the afternoon. Waiting until evening means drawing from the grid once solar production drops.

question: It is a cold January morning. Pellet consumption today is already 6.8 kg at 09:15. Is that normal?
answer: Yes, 6.8 kg by 09:15 on a day with -3.2°C outdoor temperature is within the expected range. Your 30-day average is 6.2 kg per day, but that average includes milder days. On days with temperatures below -2°C the boiler runs significantly longer to maintain the flow temperature. The solar thermal system is contributing almost nothing today — the collector is at 12.1°C with only 420W of PV production — so all thermal load is falling to the pellet boiler. Monitor throughout the day; if consumption exceeds 10 kg before evening that would warrant investigating draft settings or door/window sealing.

question: My PV yield today is already 22.1 kWh at 11:45. Is this a record and what should I do with the surplus?
answer: 22.1 kWh by 11:45 is an excellent result — it is above your 7-day average daily yield of 18.6 kWh and well above the 30-day average of 14.2 kWh. With current production at 5.12 kW and the thermal buffer already fully charged to 71.2°C throughout, this is an ideal time to run high-consumption appliances: washing machine, tumble dryer, dishwasher, or EV charging if applicable. The pellet boiler has barely run today (0.4 kg), confirming the solar thermal system is handling all hot water demand. If you have a hot water recirculation pump, now is a good time to run a legionella protection cycle if that is overdue.

question: Solar yield today is only 9.8 kWh. That seems low for September. Should I be concerned?
answer: 9.8 kWh is below your 7-day average of 14.1 kWh and well below the 30-day average of 17.4 kWh, suggesting today has had significant cloud cover or shading. The current production of only 1.24 kW at 16:30 confirms low irradiation this afternoon. However, this alone is not a cause for concern — September yields vary considerably with weather. The thermal buffer at 52.1°C is below its 7-day high of 68.4°C, which is consistent with a low-solar day, but it is still usable for domestic hot water. The pellet boiler has consumed 2.1 kg today versus a 7-day average of 1.4 kg, picking up the deficit from solar. If you see several consecutive low-yield days you may want to check the inverter for partial shading from autumn foliage.

question: It is 07:30 and the buffer top is only at 44.8°C. Will there be enough hot water for morning showers?
answer: 44.8°C at the top of the buffer is marginal for comfortable shower water. Most mixing valves require at least 55°C at the buffer outlet to deliver 38°C at the shower after mixing with cold water. The boiler is running (68.2°C) and has already consumed 1.8 kg of pellets this morning, so the buffer should be heating now. If the boiler is actively firing, the top of the buffer typically rises to 60°C within 20–30 minutes. Check whether the boiler is currently in a heating cycle — if the pump is running and the boiler temperature is stable at 68°C, you should have adequate hot water within 30 minutes. If the boiler is in standby, trigger a manual hot water priority cycle from the controller.
